chapters.title: Job loses his possessions and children

parts.text: Job is an upright, prosperous man in Uz who fears God and offers sacrifices for his children. When Satan appears before the LORD, he argues that Job serves God only because God protects and blesses him. The LORD permits Satan to touch Job’s possessions but not Job himself.

Successive messengers report the loss of Job’s livestock, servants, and all ten children through raids, fire, and a devastating wind. Job tears his clothing, shaves his head, and worships. He acknowledges that he came into the world with nothing and blesses the LORD despite his losses. He does not charge God foolishly.

chapters.title: Job’s body is afflicted

parts.text: Satan argues that Job will abandon his integrity if his own body suffers. The LORD allows the test but commands that Job’s life be spared. Struck with painful boils, Job sits among ashes and scrapes himself with a broken piece of pottery. His wife urges him to curse God and die, but he refuses, saying they must receive adversity as well as good from God.

Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar come to comfort Job. Hardly recognizing him, they weep, tear their clothes, and sit silently with him for seven days and nights because they see how great his suffering is.

chapters.title: Job laments the day of his birth

parts.text: Job breaks the silence by cursing the day of his birth and the night of his conception. He wishes that darkness would erase them from the calendar because they allowed him to enter a life filled with misery.

He asks why he did not die at birth and imagines death as rest shared by kings, prisoners, servants, and the weary. He cannot understand why life continues for those who long for death. What he feared has come upon him, leaving him without peace or rest.

chapters.title: Eliphaz argues that the innocent do not perish

parts.text: Eliphaz reminds Job that he once strengthened others with his words but now loses courage when suffering reaches him. He urges Job to rely on his reverence and integrity, then asks whether the innocent ever perish. From his own observations, he claims that those who sow wickedness reap trouble and are destroyed by God’s breath.

Eliphaz recounts a frightening night vision in which a voice questioned whether mortal people could be more righteous or pure than their Maker. He emphasizes human frailty, describing people as inhabitants of clay houses who can perish without obtaining wisdom.

chapters.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction

parts.text: Eliphaz describes the ruin of a fool and his children, insisting that trouble is part of human life. He advises Job to seek God, who sends rain, raises the lowly, frustrates the crafty, and gives hope to the poor. His counsel assumes that God’s governance explains Job’s present circumstances.

He calls the person whom God corrects happy and urges Job not to despise chastening. He promises deliverance from famine, war, slander, and destruction, along with a peaceful household, many descendants, and a full lifespan. Eliphaz presents these conclusions as truths he and his companions have investigated.

chapters.title: Job asks his friends for compassion

parts.text: Job says his grief would outweigh the sand of the sea and explains that his desperate words arise from unbearable suffering. He longs for God to end his life, yet takes comfort in not having denied God’s words. He has neither the strength nor the prospect of relief that would enable him to endure indefinitely.

He says an afflicted person deserves kindness from friends, but compares his companions to seasonal streams that disappoint thirsty travellers. He has asked them for neither money nor rescue. He invites them to identify an actual wrong, rather than treating the words of a despairing man as proof of guilt.

chapters.title: Job pleads for relief from constant suffering

parts.text: Job compares human life to hard service and describes sleepless nights, a diseased body, and days rushing away without hope. He asks God to remember how brief his life is. Like a disappearing cloud, the person who goes down to the grave does not return to his former home.

Determined to speak his anguish, Job asks why God watches him so relentlessly. Even sleep brings frightening dreams instead of comfort. He would rather die than continue in this condition and wonders why humanity receives such searching attention. He asks for pardon and a little respite before he lies in the dust.

chapters.title: Bildad appeals to inherited wisdom

parts.text: Bildad challenges Job’s words and insists that God does not pervert justice. He suggests that Job’s children were delivered over because of their sins and says that, if Job is pure and seeks God earnestly, God will restore his household and greatly increase his latter prosperity.

Appealing to earlier generations, Bildad compares the godless to plants that wither without water and to people leaning on a spider’s web. Their apparent security cannot last. He concludes that God will not reject an upright person or support evildoers, and predicts joy for Job if his condition is set right.

chapters.title: Job longs for someone to stand between him and God

parts.text: Job acknowledges God’s incomparable wisdom and power but asks how anyone can establish his case before him. God moves mountains, commands the sun, and performs wonders beyond understanding. Job feels unable to answer such a judge; even an attempt to justify himself would condemn him, and he believes his suffering has multiplied without cause.

Job protests that disaster overtakes both the innocent and the wicked while his own life races away. He cannot wash away the charges he feels against him. God is not a human opponent whom he can meet in court, and Job longs for a mediator who could remove his terror and let him speak freely.

chapters.title: Job questions why his Maker afflicts him

parts.text: Weary of life, Job asks God to explain why he contends with him. He wonders whether God judges as a limited human would, even though God knows his character. Recalling how God fashioned his body and preserved his spirit, Job struggles to reconcile that care with his present destruction.

Job imagines that God has been watching for sin and pursuing him whether he is guilty or upright. He again wishes that he had never been born. With only a short life remaining, he asks to be left alone long enough to find a little comfort before entering the darkness of death.

chapters.title: Zophar tells Job to put away wickedness

parts.text: Zophar accuses Job of excessive talk and false claims of innocence. He wishes God would answer Job directly and asserts that Job has received less punishment than his wrongdoing deserves. God’s wisdom, he argues, is beyond human discovery, and no one can obstruct God’s judgment or hide wickedness from him.

He tells Job to prepare his heart, pray, and remove sin from his life and household. Zophar promises that repentance will bring confidence, brightness, security, and forgetfulness of past misery. He contrasts this hoped-for restoration with the wicked, whose expectations fail and whose only remaining hope is death.

chapters.title: Job describes God’s rule over human power

parts.text: Job rejects his friends’ claim to superior wisdom. He understands their arguments but observes that robbers prosper while a just person becomes an object of mockery. Animals, birds, earth, and fish bear witness that every living creature depends on the LORD, so God’s sovereignty is not a discovery peculiar to his counsellors.

Job describes God overturning the structures people trust: counsellors lose wisdom, judges become fools, kings are unbound, and priests are led away spoiled. God enlarges nations and destroys them, reveals hidden things, and deprives rulers of understanding. Human status and apparent success cannot place anyone beyond his power.

chapters.title: Job demands an honest hearing

parts.text: Job says he knows as much as his friends and wants to reason with God himself. He calls them useless physicians and asks whether they intend to defend God by speaking falsely. Their biased arguments will not survive God’s examination. Despite the danger, Job resolves to present his case and hopes for salvation.

He asks God to withdraw the affliction and terror that prevent a fair hearing, then invites God either to question him or answer him. He wants to know his transgressions and why he is treated as an enemy. Job compares himself to a driven leaf and decaying clothing under relentless scrutiny.

chapters.title: Job considers human frailty and the hope of renewal

parts.text: Job describes human life as brief, troubled, and unable to escape its appointed limits. He asks God to turn from humanity long enough to allow some rest. A cut tree may sprout again when watered, but a person dies and disappears from the familiar world, as waters dry up from a river.

Job wishes that God would hide him in the grave until anger had passed, then remember and call him. He asks whether a dead person will live again and imagines answering his Maker. Yet his complaint returns to the wearing away of hope: people die without knowing what later happens to their children.

chapters.title: Eliphaz accuses Job of arrogant speech

parts.text: Eliphaz says Job’s answers are empty and undermine reverence for God. He treats Job’s own words as evidence against him and asks whether Job possesses wisdom denied to the aged. Eliphaz repeats his argument that no human being can claim purity before God, who finds imperfection even in the heavens.

He describes the wicked as tormented by fear, haunted by impending destruction, and defiant against the Almighty. Their wealth cannot endure, and they will be like trees losing their fruit before its season.

chapters.title: Job seeks a witness beyond his friends

parts.text: Job calls his companions miserable comforters. If their situations were reversed, he says, he could strengthen them instead of multiplying accusations. He depicts his suffering as an assault in which God and hostile people have broken him down, although he maintains that his hands are free from violence and his prayer is pure.

He calls on the earth not to conceal his blood or silence his cry. While his friends scorn him, he declares that his witness is in heaven and pours out tears to God. He longs for someone to plead a person’s case before God, knowing that his remaining years will soon carry him toward death.

chapters.title: Job finds little hope in his companions’ promises

parts.text: Job says his spirit is broken and the grave is ready, while mockers surround him. He asks God to provide the security that no one else will give. His humiliation has astonished upright people, yet he says the righteous will hold to their way and the clean-handed will grow stronger.

He challenges his friends to try again, finding no wise answer among them. His purposes have been shattered, and their language turns night into day without changing his condition. If he must look to the grave as his house and worms as his family, he asks where any visible hope remains.

chapters.title: Bildad pictures the ruin of the wicked

parts.text: Bildad angrily asks why Job treats his companions as ignorant and whether the world’s order should be overturned for his sake. He describes the wicked person’s light going out, strength failing, and steps leading into traps. Hidden snares surround a life that once seemed secure.

Terror follows the wicked, disease consumes them, and they are driven from their dwelling to the king of terrors. Their memory, descendants, and home disappear, leaving observers appalled. Bildad concludes that this is the fate of those who do not know God.

chapters.title: Job affirms that his redeemer lives

parts.text: Job asks how long his friends will torment him with accusations. He says God has fenced in his path and stripped away his honour, while relatives, servants, children, and close companions have turned against him. Reduced almost to skin and bones, he pleads for pity rather than further pursuit.

He wishes his words could be permanently recorded and declares that his redeemer lives and will stand at the latter day upon the earth. Though his body is destroyed, he expects to see God for himself. He warns those persecuting him to fear the sword and remember that there is a judgment.

chapters.title: Zophar describes wickedness as short-lived pleasure

parts.text: Zophar feels compelled to answer what he regards as Job’s insulting rebuke. He insists that the triumph of the wicked is brief, however high they rise. Their children lose their security, their strength vanishes, and the evil they once savored becomes deadly within them, like food turning to poison.

He says ill-gotten wealth must be surrendered and that oppression of the poor brings hunger, distress, and divine anger. Escape from one weapon only exposes the wicked to another; darkness and fire consume what remains. Heaven reveals their iniquity and earth rises against them. Zophar presents this destruction as the inheritance God appoints to a wicked person.

chapters.title: Job points to the prosperity of the wicked

parts.text: Job asks his friends to listen before continuing their mockery. Contrary to their descriptions, he observes wicked people living long, powerful lives, with secure homes, thriving livestock, happy children, and pleasant music. They reject the need to serve God yet may go suddenly to the grave. Job himself refuses their counsel, but insists that their prosperity must be faced honestly.

Job considers the destruction of the wicked and punishment reaching their children, then observes that people with very different lives lie together in death. He challenges his friends’ accusations and appeals to travellers’ testimony. The wicked face a day of wrath, yet are brought to the grave, with innumerable people before and after them. Job concludes that his friends’ comfort is empty and their answers contain falsehood.

chapters.title: Eliphaz supplies accusations and promises restoration

parts.text: Eliphaz now directly accuses Job of taking unjust pledges, withholding food and water, and mistreating widows and orphans. He says these offences explain Job’s terror and darkness. He warns against imagining that God’s height prevents him from seeing human behaviour and recalls the destruction of earlier evildoers.

He urges Job to make peace with God, receive instruction, put away wrongdoing, and delight in the Almighty. Eliphaz promises restored prosperity, answered prayer, and light on Job’s path. He even speaks of deliverance extending to others through clean hands.

chapters.title: Job searches for God and maintains his integrity

parts.text: Job longs to find God’s judgment seat and set out his arguments. He believes God would hear rather than crush an upright person, but cannot locate him in any direction. His complaint is intensified by the apparent absence of the judge before whom he wishes to speak.

Nevertheless, Job says God knows his way and that, when tried, he will come forth like gold. He has followed God’s steps and valued his words more than necessary food. Yet God’s unchangeable purpose frightens him: no one can turn him aside, and Job cannot understand the appointed suffering that still lies before him.

chapters.title: Job describes injustice that seems unpunished

parts.text: Job asks why those who know God do not see clear times of judgment. He lists stolen landmarks and livestock, exploitation of orphans and widows, and the misery of labourers left hungry, thirsty, and exposed. Murderers, adulterers, and thieves use darkness to conceal their acts, while the wounded cry out without an obvious answer.

The closing descriptions speak of evildoers’ disappearance and the cutting down of the mighty, yet Job continues to challenge easy explanations of their apparent security. God sees their ways even when they are allowed to rest confidently for a time. Job ends by asking who can prove his account false.

chapters.title: Bildad contrasts God’s majesty with human uncleanness

parts.text: Bildad gives a brief answer centred on God’s overwhelming dominion. God establishes peace in his high places, commands unnumbered armies, and shines his light upon everyone. Against that majesty, Bildad asks how anyone born of a woman can be justified or clean before God. Even the moon and stars, he says, are not pure in God’s sight. He closes by comparing human beings to worms.

chapters.title: Job describes wonders beyond human understanding

parts.text: Job responds sarcastically to Bildad, asking how his words have helped the powerless or brought wisdom to the ignorant. He challenges the source and usefulness of this supposed counsel. The exchange exposes the gap between grand statements about God and the comfort or explanation Job has requested.

Job then describes God’s power over the depths, the heavens, the suspended earth, clouds, sea, and the boundaries of light and darkness. The pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke, and his spirit adorns the heavens. Yet these wonders are only the edges of God’s ways, a faint whisper compared with the thunder of his power.

chapters.title: Job refuses a false confession

parts.text: Job swears that, while he lives, he will not speak deceit or concede that his friends’ accusations are right. Though he believes God has made his life bitter, he holds fast to his righteousness and refuses to surrender his integrity. He contrasts this determination with the hopelessness of the hypocrite who cannot rely on God in trouble.

Job describes the inheritance of the wicked: children meet the sword or hunger, accumulated wealth passes to the just, and fragile houses collapse. Terror and a violent storm carry the evildoer away. These descriptions do not become a confession that Job committed the crimes his companions have alleged.

chapters.title: Wisdom cannot be bought or mined

parts.text: Job describes human skill in mining hidden treasures. People dig deep into the earth, cut channels through rock, and uncover silver, gold, iron, precious stones, and things concealed from birds and beasts. Their ingenuity reaches places ordinarily hidden from sight, overturning mountains to bring buried riches into the light.

Wisdom, however, cannot be located or purchased like these materials. Neither the depths nor the sea possesses it, and the finest jewels cannot equal its price. God alone understands its way, for he sees all creation and established the forces of nature. For humanity, fearing the Lord is wisdom, and departing from evil is understanding.

chapters.title: Job remembers former honour and usefulness

parts.text: Job wishes for the days when God’s care seemed visibly present, his children surrounded him, and his household flourished. Elders and princes respected him, and people welcomed his words. He remembers rescuing the poor, helping the orphan and widow, and defending the rights of those who needed protection.

He had expected to grow old securely, with lasting honour and renewed strength. Others waited quietly for his counsel and received it as welcome rain. He encouraged them with his presence and guided them like a chief among his people. The recollection emphasizes the contrast between a life of service and his present rejection.

chapters.title: Job contrasts his former life with present humiliation

parts.text: Job says men younger and less respected than those who once honoured him now mock and spit at him. People driven to the margins of society have made him their song. He feels exposed to an advancing assault as his dignity and security disappear and terror overwhelms him.

His pain continues day and night, and he cries to God without receiving the answer he seeks. Having once wept for others in trouble, he expected good but has received evil. He describes himself as a companion of desolate creatures, his skin darkened, his bones burning, and the music of his life turned into mourning.

chapters.title: Job presents an oath of innocence

parts.text: Job reviews his conduct under solemn conditions, beginning with a covenant against lustful looking. He denies deceit, adultery, and injustice toward servants, recognizing that their Maker is also his. He says he fed the hungry, clothed the poor, cared for orphans and widows, and feared God’s judgment if he abused his power.

He rejects confidence in wealth, worship of the heavenly lights, rejoicing over an enemy’s downfall, and hiding wrongdoing through fear of others. He asks that an accuser produce a written charge so he can answer openly. He even invokes judgment on himself if his land was gained through exploitation. With this appeal, Job’s words end.

chapters.title: Elihu explains why he will speak

parts.text: Elihu becomes angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and with the three friends for condemning Job without answering him. Because he is younger, he has waited while the older men spoke. He now argues that understanding comes from God’s spirit rather than age alone and says he has listened without finding a convincing reply.

Unable to remain silent, Elihu compares his inward pressure to wine in sealed skins ready to burst. He intends to speak frankly without flattering anyone or showing partiality. He warns himself that his Maker could quickly remove him if he used flattering titles to gain favour.

chapters.title: Elihu describes God’s warnings and deliverance

parts.text: Elihu asks Job to listen and assures him that he is a fellow creature made from clay, not someone whose power should terrify him. He recalls Job’s claims of cleanness and his complaint that God treats him as an enemy. Elihu argues that God is greater than humanity and need not explain every action to people.

He says God speaks through dreams and painful chastening to turn people from pride and preserve them from destruction. He describes a messenger, a ransom, restored health, prayer, and confession bringing deliverance from the pit. Elihu presents these as ways God repeatedly seeks a person’s rescue and invites Job either to answer or to hear more.

chapters.title: Elihu defends God’s justice

parts.text: Elihu invites the listeners to examine his argument. He repeats Job’s complaint that God has denied him justice and criticizes what he takes to be a claim that serving God brings no benefit. God cannot act wickedly, Elihu insists: all life depends upon him, and his authority is not delegated by a superior.

God sees every human step, overturns rulers without partiality, and hears the oppressed. Elihu urges the proper response to chastening to be a request for instruction and a promise to abandon wrongdoing. He concludes that Job has spoken without understanding and wishes his testing to continue because, in Elihu’s judgment, Job adds rebellion to sin.

chapters.title: Elihu questions Job’s expectations of God

parts.text: Elihu challenges Job’s concern about what advantage righteousness brings. Looking toward the heavens, he argues that human sin cannot diminish God and human righteousness does not supply something God lacks. Wickedness and righteousness do, however, affect other people. God’s greatness prevents anyone from treating him as a dependent party in an exchange.

Elihu says the oppressed often cry out without seeking their Maker, who gives songs in the night and wisdom beyond that of animals. He connects unanswered cries with pride and empty appeals. He urges Job to wait for God’s judgment and concludes that Job has multiplied words without knowledge.

chapters.title: Elihu urges Job to learn from affliction

parts.text: Elihu continues defending God’s righteousness. He says God watches the righteous and uses affliction to expose wrongdoing and open ears to correction. Those who obey may prosper, while those who reject instruction perish. Elihu applies this warning to Job, urging him not to turn toward iniquity or imagine that wealth or power could purchase escape.

He calls Job to magnify God’s work rather than accuse his ways. God’s greatness exceeds human knowledge, and the years of his life cannot be counted. Elihu points to evaporation, rain, clouds, lightning, and thunder as manifestations of a power that both supplies food and governs judgment.

chapters.title: Elihu points to the wonder of storms

parts.text: Elihu trembles at thunder, describing it as the voice of God’s majesty. Snow, rain, frost, and storms interrupt human work and send animals into shelter. Clouds move according to God’s counsel, bringing what he appoints for correction, for the land, or for mercy.

He urges Job to stand still and consider these wonders. Can Job explain the balancing of clouds or spread out the sky? Elihu acknowledges that people cannot adequately order their speech before such greatness. The Almighty exceeds discovery, possesses power and abundant justice, and does not afflict unjustly. Therefore people should fear him rather than trust their own wisdom.

chapters.title: The LORD questions Job about creation

parts.text: The LORD answers Job from a whirlwind and challenges words spoken without knowledge. He asks where Job was when the earth was founded, who established the sea’s boundaries, and whether Job has commanded the morning. Further questions concern the depths, the gates of death, and the dwelling places of light and darkness.

The questioning continues through snow, hail, rain, ice, stars, clouds, and lightning. Job cannot account for the governing of these things or provide the wisdom behind them. The LORD also asks who supplies prey for lions and food for young ravens, directing attention to care that extends beyond human control.

chapters.title: The LORD questions Job about wild creatures

parts.text: The LORD asks whether Job knows the birth seasons of mountain goats and deer or governs their young. He describes the freedom of the wild ass and the untamable strength of the unicorn, questioning whether Job could use such creatures for ordinary farm work. The ostrich’s treatment of her eggs and remarkable speed likewise lie outside Job’s ordering.

The LORD then describes the war horse, fearless amid weapons and eager at the sound of battle. He asks whether Job gives the hawk its flight or commands the eagle to nest on high and find prey. The creatures display abilities and ways that Job neither designed nor directs.

chapters.title: Job is silenced and shown behemoth

parts.text: The LORD asks whether Job will instruct the Almighty, and Job acknowledges his lowliness, placing his hand over his mouth. The LORD continues: will Job condemn God in order to justify himself? If Job possesses divine power, let him humble every proud person and destroy the wicked; then his ability to save himself would be demonstrated.

The LORD directs Job to behemoth, a powerful creature he made alongside humanity. It eats grass, has immense bodily strength, and rests among reeds and shaded places. Untroubled by the rushing river, it presents another example of created power beyond Job’s mastery, while remaining subject to its Maker.

chapters.title: The LORD describes leviathan

parts.text: The LORD asks whether Job can catch leviathan, tame it, make it a servant, or treat it as a pet. Any attempt to confront it reveals the inadequacy of human strength. If people cannot safely stir this creature, they have still less ground for standing against its Maker, who owns everything beneath heaven.

Leviathan’s formidable teeth, tightly joined scales, fiery breath, strength, and resistance to weapons are described in vivid detail. It churns the sea and leaves a shining wake. Leviathan is made without fear and is king over all the children of pride.

chapters.title: Job repents and the LORD restores him

parts.text: Job acknowledges God’s power and confesses that he spoke about things beyond his understanding. Having encountered the LORD, he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two companions for not speaking rightly about him as Job has, and directs them to offer sacrifices while Job prays for them.

The LORD restores Job as he prays for his friends and gives him twice his former possessions. Relatives return to comfort and help him. He has seven sons and three daughters, whose inheritance is granted alongside their brothers. Job lives another 140 years, sees four generations, and dies old and full of days.
